questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x)
$$

on $[-1,1]$, where $f$ is $2$-periodic and odd. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $2$-periodic on $[-1,1]$, we have $L=1$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis 

$$
cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{1})\,\text{and}\,sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{1}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a sine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-4,4]$, where $f$ is $8$-periodic and odd. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $8$-periodic on $[-4,4]$, we have $L=4$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis 

$$
cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{4})\,\text{and}\,sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{4}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a sine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4})
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-1,1]$, where $f$ is $2$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $2$-periodic on $[-1,1]$, we have $L=1$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7y=f(x)
$$

on $[-5,5]$, where $f$ is $10$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $10$-periodic on $[-5,5]$, we have $L=5$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=3
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+4y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$
